title: Brain tumour diagnosis cut from weeks to hours with rapid new NHS test
description: A rapid new test for brain tumours that the NHS has started using can slash the time it takes for an accurate diagnosis from up to eight weeks to two
body: A rapid new test for brain tumours that the NHS has started using can slash the time it takes for an accurate diagnosis from up to eight weeks to two hours.  The test, which is used by doctors to diagnose which type of tumour a patient has, should mean patients can start treatment including radiotherapy and chemotherapy sooner, and are spared weeks of uncertainty.Steve Palmer, 55, from Nottingham, is among those to benefit from the new technology - and it meant surgeons were able to get his result while they were still operating to remove his tumour."Getting that quick diagnosis removed weeks of anxiety," he told the BBC.NHS England said that the genomic test, which works by quickly analysing the genetic code of a sample of the tumour, will be piloted in specialist centres around England.There are around 150 different types of brain tumour ranging from slow-growing to aggressive cancers, each of which can respond differently to treatment.Steve was diagnosed with a brain tumour after he collapsed at the gym, and the test revealed it to be a grade 4 glioblastoma. "It wasn't the result I wanted to hear but it means I can get on with the next phase of treatment and recovery, and get on with fighting whatever it is I've got to fight," he told the BBC.Consultant neurosurgeon Stuart Smith, who led Steve's operation at Queens Medical Centre, part of Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust, told the BBC the test "seems almost magical.""The diagnosis of brain tumours relies on molecular and genetic analysis but it can take up to six to eight weeks to get the full information back. Here it is done while we are still operating."Diagnosing the type of tumour while the patient is still on the operating table could impact how surgeons operate. Smith explained: "For some tumour types, which are curable, surgery needs to be as radical as possible to remove every last bit of tumour that we can find.  "Other types, sadly, are too aggressive, and beyond what surgery can remove, so we would be more cautious in order to lower the risk of causing damage to the brain."The test works by sending small tissue samples taken from the tumour to the pathology lab. The samples are prepared for loading into a shoebox-sized sequencing machine made by Oxford Nanopore, which uses specialist software developed at the University of Nottingham, in partnership with hospital clinicians. The molecules of DNA pass through a nanopore - a tiny hole - which reveals the tumour's unique genomic fingerprint.In Steve's case, after the nanopore machine was running for 20 minutes, the neuropathology team called the theatre to tell them that the tumour was likely to be a glioblastoma.Dr Simon Paine, consultant neuropathologist at Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust, explained that the genomic test was transformative in comparison to what he could determine by looking at tumour cells down a microscope."I'm crystal ball gazing and can do it reasonably well on a good day, but nowhere near with the clarity of the nanopore, which gives a comprehensive molecular classification," he said.More than 12,000 people in the UK are diagnosed with a primary brain tumour each year. It is the biggest cancer killer of children and adults under 40.Prof Frankie Swords, NHS medical director, said: "For people with suspected brain tumours, getting the right diagnosis quickly can feel like a race against time, while waiting weeks for answers can be agonising for them and their families."This remarkable rapid test has the potential to completely transform how we diagnose brain tumours, with results reaching patients in a matter of days rather than weeks."This is a huge leap forward for patients - a faster diagnosis means they can start the right treatment or access clinical trials sooner, while for some patients it could mean surgeons can make potentially life-changing decisions about their surgery while on the operating table."Speaking to BBC Breakfast, she called the pilot scheme a "world first" and said "no other health service" is rolling the technology out across multiple hospitals. The NHS England pilot will involve five specialist centres in Nottingham, Birmingham, London and Newcastle - they are Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust, University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust, Great Ormond Street Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, King's College Hospital and Newcastle Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust.It will later be extended to sites in Bristol, Oxford, Leeds and Manchester.The pilot builds on an earlier project already under way in Nottingham and Birmingham.

schema.headline: Brain tumour diagnosis cut from weeks to hours with rapid new NHS test

title: Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas charged after dinghy slashed in Channel
description: Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been charged with criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at a dinghy in the English Chann
body: Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been charged with criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at a dinghy in the English Channel.The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, has also been charged with failing to disclose the PIN to his phone, Hampshire Police said.He has been remanded in custody and is due to appear at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court via videolink on Friday, the force added.Several hundred people had gathered outside a police investigation centre in Basingstoke on Thursday evening believing Thomas was inside.The demonstration, which seemed to pass off peacefully, began shortly before 18:30 BST. Protesters stood on the road outside the building and could be heard chanting "free DT".The crowd began to disperse at about 21:45 BST after they learned of the charges against Thomas.

schema.headline: Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas charged after dinghy slashed in Channel

title: Xi Jinping got the red carpet treatment from Trump - but not everything he wanted
description: Figure caption, Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go?ByLaura BickerChina correspondentPresident Xi Jinping's summits with
body: Figure caption, Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go?ByLaura BickerChina correspondentPresident Xi Jinping's summits with Donald Trump have one clear aim.China believes the United States is trying to contain its rise as a superpower, and it wants Washington to stay out of its way - particularly when it comes to trade, technology and Taiwan.On this visit, however, despite Trump rolling out the red carpet for him, the Chinese leader didn't get everything he wanted.The trade truce that saw both countries pause a tit-for-tat tariff war and prevent a further escalation, was extended by only a few months - from November to January.Beijing had hoped for at least a year as Xi looks to ride out the remainder of Trump's presidency.This means key disputes on tariffs, China's dominance on rare earth supplies and access to advanced US chips are being kicked forward into yet another round of negotiations.This suggests the US wants China to do more to fulfil its side of the bargain before offering longer-term concessions.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Trump and Xi attend a dinner at the White HouseThe uncomfortable truth for Xi is that his domestic economy is in trouble. While the country sells a record number of goods around the world, consumers at home are holding back. Youth unemployment remains stubbornly high and property prices have slumped in a country where 80% of people own their own homes.Trade is helping to prop up growth, making access to overseas markets more important than ever. Xi needs to protect those exports from the kind of debilitating tariffs the US imposed last year.On Taiwan, Xi once again made clear that US arms sales to Taiwan are a red line for China.The US is bound by law to provide the self-governing island with the means to defend itself.In May, Xi warned Trump that mishandling the issue could cause the two countries to "collide or even enter into conflict".Trump then delayed the approval of a $14 billion arms package for Taiwan, describing it as a "very good negotiating chip" with Beijing.Xi may have seized on that opening during the talks and likely argued that restraining support for Taiwan reduces the risk of conflict.On Thursday he reiterated his hope that the US would adhere to the "correct position" of opposing Taiwan independence.However,  Trump - who is coming under some bipartisan pressure to continue US support to Taiwan - is yet to make any public response to the Chinese leader's comments.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Trade is helping to prop up growthThe two leaders did at least discuss artificial intelligence (AI) although it's unclear whether they agreed to any safeguards.All eyes were on whether they would make any concrete decisions on AI - such as an agreement to hold a summit - in the wake of an essay by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calling for the slowing down of AI development to make it safer. That followed a warning by a top safety researcher from the company that there was a "greater than 10% chance" that AI could cause the extinction of humans.But besides Xi talking about the importance of ensuring AI "is always under human control" we didn't get much else. Trump has most recently dismissed fears of human extinction from the technology as a "hoax".And, of course, let's not forget the pandas. The gift of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang to Atlanta was first heralded in April, but Xi has now announced they will arrive in just a few days as China's panda diplomacy resumes.There may be more announcements to come as the two prepare to have tea and visit the national archives on Friday.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Pandas have played an important role in Chinese diplomatic measuresBut for now, one of the summit's biggest victories for Beijing may have been the optics.The lavish welcome, a personal greeting at the airport and a state banquet featuring sesame crusted sea bass and braised baby bok choy have been welcomed by those watching from China. It will have helped cement Xi's image at home as Trump's equal.Memes contrasting the two leaders have spread widely on Chinese social media. One popular image shows Trump grimacing as bomber jets fly overhead, while Xi remained impassive.Xi has found a way to manage one of the world's most unpredictable leaders. But while Trump talks of a "truly great friendship", China's leader is focussed on something bigger: securing China's place alongside the United States as a superpower.The pandas, the pageantry and the warm words may help smooth this relationship. But beneath the spectacle, the competition between the world's two most powerful countries remains as fierce as ever.

schema.headline: Xi Jinping got the red carpet treatment from Trump - but not everything he wanted

title: Italy ministers agree to ban burqa and niqab in school and cap foreigners in class
description: The Italian government has approved a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools, along with a limit on the share of pupils who speak little Italian in any
body: The Italian government has approved a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools, along with a limit on the share of pupils who speak little Italian in any one class. A 30% cap will be imposed on children without Italian citizenship or poor knowledge of the Italian language in the first year of primary, middle and high school.Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni described the measures as "common-sense tools that do not divide but really help to integrate".Opposition parties accuse the government of pandering to the policies of the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party, ahead of a general election next year.Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara has said the limit is "purely linguistic" rather than one of citizenship, while he has sought to frame the ban on the niqab and burqa as a matter of gender equality."You must go to school with your face uncovered," Meloni said while announcing the plans on Sunday, adding that no-one could decide that a young woman should hide herself in the name of tradition.There were several drafts of the decree ahead of Thursday's council of ministers meeting, however the core details were clear.The veil ban would apply to the burqa and niqab, but not the hijab, which leaves the face visible. The niqab is a veil for the face that leaves the area around the eyes clear. However, it may be worn with a separate eye veil. It is worn with an accompanying headscarf.The burka is a one-piece veil that covers the face and body. Often there is a mesh screen around the eyes to see through.Non-Italian citizens make up 11.6% of pupils in Italy's schools, according to the research institution Fondazione ISMU.The 30% limit on pupils who speak limited Italian will cover separate stages of education differently.In primary schools, it would cover non-Italian citizens who have either not been born in Italy or who have not attended at least two years of nursery school. In lower- and upper- secondary schools, it would cover pupils without Italian citizenship who have not successfully completed at least three years in the Italian school system.Local school offices would be asked to spread pupils with little Italian language skills more evenly among nearby schools. Where that is not possible, exemptions would apply, with extra Italian teaching. The aim was to avoid "ghetto classes", the education minister explained.The draft also goes further on parents, according to the Ansa news agency. Schools would have to report to social services cases in which persistent language barriers among those with parental responsibility hinder a child's integration. Free Italian courses would be offered.The measure is a decree law, meaning it can take effect immediately, but must be ratified by parliament within 60 days.Italy already has guidance on Italian language at schools. A 2010 ministerial notice under then-Education Minister Mariastella Gelmini set a 30% limit "as a rule" on pupils without Italian citizenship. The new decree puts the limit into law.The political opposition says the plan is as much about politics as schools. Opponents accuse Meloni of pandering to Roberto Vannacci, a retired military general who leads the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party and is seen as a threat to the governing coalition's right flank.The leader of the centre-left Democratic Party (PD), Elly Schlein, called the plan propaganda and impossible to implement. PD deputy and chamber vice-president Anna Ascani also accused the government of propaganda at the expense of schoolchildren.Valditara, speaking by video link from New York at a press conference rejected the charge. "We are not chasing Vannacci; if anything, he is chasing us," he said.Vannacci said he agreed with the measures, but they should have come years ago. The League's Matteo Salvini, who launched a separate package of measures on what he called "political Islam" on Wednesday, accused Vannacci of "continually voting against the government".Salvini said he hoped Futuro Nazionale would back the League's new proposals.

schema.headline: Italy ministers agree to ban burqa and niqab in school and cap foreigners in class

title: Media outlets banned by Trump denied access to White House event despite judge's order
description: CNN and MS NOW reporters say they have been denied entry to cover a White House state dinner despite a judge ruling their access to the grounds must b
body: CNN and MS NOW reporters say they have been denied entry to cover a White House state dinner despite a judge ruling their access to the grounds must be restored.A federal judge said in an overnight ruling that the White House ban on three outlets - CNN and MS NOW and Politico - was likely unconstitutional and that the administration must allow them access, for now. Trump barred them last week, accusing them of "fake news".Journalists with the three outlets were allowed back in on Thursday morning. Then in the evening, a CNN reporter and a producer and an MS NOW reporter said that they were denied entry to cover the guests arriving for a state dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping.The outlets said they had properly submitted their reporters' names for credentials to cover the arrivals.CNN said that about an hour before Xi was scheduled to arrive, the White House said it could cover the event only with a photojournalist and audio technician, but not a team that included a reporter and producer.MS NOW White House reporter Laura Barron-Lopez said she was told by White House staff that she could not be let in, and to contact the White House communications director.The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.A White House communications account posted on X that "contrary to what the Fake News wants you to believe, they don't just get to have free rein into every part of the White House, every event, and every press call".The incident was the latest in a series of events on Thursday surrounding the ban on some media outlets at the White House.Despite the overnight ruling, CNN, Politico and MS NOW all reported being denied entry to the White House on Thursday morning, prompting a request for an emergency court hearing.In response, the director of White House Operations said in a court filing that the press passes and confiscated badges had been restored by 09:45 local time (13:45 GMT). Shortly afterwards, all three outlets said they were allowed back in.However, networks including Fox News, NBC, CBS and ABC, which pulled out in solidarity, have yet to confirm they will resume broadcast coverage from the White House.The chaotic standoff limited some TV coverage as Trump welcomed Xi to the White House ahead of a state dinner. In his ruling, Judge Timothy Kelly said the ban on the outlets should be temporarily lifted because it "likely violated their constitutional due process rights".He cast doubt on White House claims that the ban was justified in part on national security grounds, pointing out the president made no mention of this in his initial announcement."The record lacks factual support for defendants' contention that the revocation of plaintiffs' hard passes will in fact protect national security," Kelly wrote.Judge Kelly ruled CNN, Politico and MS NOW were "likely to succeed" in showing the White House had not exercised "adequate due process" in the ban.He ordered the immediate return of the outlets' press passes and a halt to enforcement of the ban for 14 days.In a court filing on Tuesday, the US Department of Justice had accused the news outlets of threatening national security with their coverage. Government lawyers cited stories about missile stockpiles, the construction of the White House ballroom and the recent Republican midterm convention.Trump first announced last Friday he was barring the three outlets from the White House, accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration. By Saturday morning, each outlet reported that they were denied entry to the White House grounds and that their press badges were confiscated. All three outlets accused the Trump administration of violating their constitutional rights.In a joint statement on Monday, they said they were pursuing legal action to "defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports".More than 50 media organisations across the ideological spectrum filed an amicus brief in support of the lawsuit, including Fox News, the New York Times, the Washington Post and the Wall Street Journal. There have been previous instances of administrations attempting to limit certain outlets' access.The Obama administration tried to exclude Fox News from participating in a specific press pool interview with an administration official in 2009.But after objections from the other four networks in the press pool, Fox News was allowed in.

schema.headline: Media outlets banned by Trump denied access to White House event despite judge's order

title: Victims 'grossly failed' by Zafer Dogan bail decision
description: Victims and their families were "grossly failed" by the court system that bailed a sex offender and repeatedly allowed him to return to his home overl
body: Victims and their families were "grossly failed" by the court system that bailed a sex offender and repeatedly allowed him to return to his home overlooking the playground he targeted, London's victims' commissioner said.Zafer Dogan, 32, of Enfield, north London, was jailed on Thursday for two years and four months for taking thousands of pictures of children and using AI software to "nudify" them.Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today, Andrea Simon said the case showed that "the justice system did not centre victims" and called for a multi-agency review.A government spokesperson said the law was clear that bail "should only be used where necessary and proportionate, including to protect victims".Dogan had pleaded guilty to three counts of making indecent images of a child, which included 900 category C images, 294 category B images and 653 category A images, which are the most serious.He also admitted possessing extreme pornography, possessing a prohibited image of a child, creating purported intimate images of an adult, obstructing a constable in the execution of their duty and a further two counts of making indecent photographs of a child.According to the police, he had taken more than 5,000 pictures, many from his bedroom window.Despite protests from the police and prosecutors, he had previously been bailed back to his flat, forcing one family who had fallen victim to his crimes to move into temporary accommodation.Simon said: "I think victims and their families were grossly failed by the decision to allow this paedophile to return to an address where he was overlooking a playground near to his victims."The case [shows that] the justice system just does not centre victims. To know that the police and prosecutors opposed bail multiple times, but nevertheless, he was returned to the community, is an indication that the capacity pressures on prisons are not being balanced with the impacts that that's having on victims' lives."We seem to be lurching from one crisis to another, and victim safety and their rights seem to be put to one side, as the justice system struggles."Simon's criticism was echoed by Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley who said it was "unfathomable" that Dogan was ever granted bail.Sir Mark said: "Prosecutors rightly opposed bail on multiple occasions, building on officers' clear assessments of the great risk he posed, and yet bail decisions were ultimately made that prioritised the offender's interests over the safety and the peace of mind of the victims."A victim and their family found themselves living in close proximity to a man who had admitted targeting them."They were so fearful, they ultimately felt forced to move to distant temporary accommodation, disrupting their lives and disrupting their children's lives, simply to escape being in the neighbourhood of the offender."He also criticised "some grossly irresponsible technology and AI companies"."Dogan voyeuristically photographed children known to him before using an AI photo-editing technology to manipulate those images for his own sexual gratification," he said."Companies must do more to prevent their platforms and tools from being used to facilitate sexual offending and harm."Simon said there were parallels to be drawn with the case of serial sex offender and murderer Simon Levy.Levy killed two women and raped a third in 2025 while on bail for other offences, after a series of decisions by authorities that left him free to roam the streets. Levy had been reported to the Metropolitan Police for a sexual assault in 2017. He then assaulted two women in 2018, but was only convicted for those offences in 2021.After being released from prison - where he sexually assaulted a female officer - he committed other assaults before the 2025 murders.He was sentenced to life in prison in August.Sir Mark previously described that case as a "whole system failing", criticising the decision of the courts and Crown Prosecution Service to bail Levy.Simon also raised concerns over the government's early release scheme which is set to see about  2,550 eligible offenders leaving jails in England and Wales by the end of the year."I hear from victims about what they think they want to do ahead of offenders' early releases from prison," she said, " they feel they may have to install security cameras or change their daily routines, or live in fear."Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

schema.headline: Victims 'grossly failed' by Zafer Dogan bail decision

title: New policies, election speculation: What to expect from Burnham's first Labour conference as PM
description: Andy Burnham had plenty to say about where the government - and the country - was going wrong at last year's Labour conference in Liverpool.But that w
body: Andy Burnham had plenty to say about where the government - and the country - was going wrong at last year's Labour conference in Liverpool.But that was at a fringe meeting on the sidelines of the main event.Now, as Labour leader and prime minister, he is the main event - and it is down to him to show party members and the wider public that he has some answers.Earlier this week, he said his debut leader's speech would leave nobody in any doubt about "what I'm trying to do in this role"."People are going to know the direction I want to take this country and I will set it down quite clearly," he told reporters en route to the UN General Assembly in New York.An internal No 10 note has set out the broad themes he will explore when he takes to the stage in Liverpool on Tuesday - including setting out long-term solutions to build a belief that the future can be brighter.The slogan for this year's conference is "Hope Again".So in his speech he is likely to point to his forthcoming 10 Year Plan for the UK – which, he says, will have "making life more affordable" at its core.As for the specifics of what he will say, some of it will be very familiar to anyone who was listening to his conference fringe speech 12 months ago.Back then, he declared then that the country had "lost control" of "the essentials" following the Thatcher-era sell off of utilities and that we were all "overpaying for  water, housing  energy, transport".He called for a renewed emphasis on technical education and wanted to see a decade of council house building on the scale of the post-war Labour government.For a politician frequently denounced for "flip flopping" he has been remarkably consistent in recent times.He is likely to re-alight on themes from his Labour leadership campaign – saying more about his commitment to greater "public control" – though not necessarily public ownership - of life's necessities; building national resilience in an unstable world; and investing political capital in the reform of social care.  A potential crowd pleaser would be to tell Labour activists from the main stage what he told them as Greater Manchester mayor from the fringe last year – that he will set up a commission to examine electoral reform.Such a move would be supported by about a quarter of his own MPs and would tie in with his leadership campaign promise of "a new politics", focused on "problem solving" rather than "point scoring".We are also likely to hear more about getting young people into work or training, with the conclusions of the review by the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn likely to be published soon.And there is certain to be plenty about his efforts to devolve power away from Whitehall to England's mayors and the new No 10 North.The task for Burnham is to meld these snapshots into a compelling and coherent narrative, culminating in a vision of the Britain he wants to see a decade from now.But there are already worries that this might become a fictional narrative unless he also focuses even more on the here and now. After all, Sir Keir Starmer's "decade of national renewal" was binned after just two bumpy years in office.Party insiders say measures such as removing VAT from electricity bills are just the start of that assistance.But Labour's biggest union funder, Unite, wants to see much more robust action on living costs sooner rather than later.  The union does not want the promise of jam tomorrow, but some instant sweeteners.Its leader, Sharon Graham, has called for a "winter fuel in reverse" – a policy from Burnham next week which would be as popular as Starmer's early removal of payments from many pensioners was unpopular.The union has put forward a motion which gives the PM plenty of options such as a cap on energy prices and unfreezing tax thresholds – an issue Burnham himself said had come up on the doorsteps when he was campaigning to be the MP for Makerfield. The union has said revenue can be raised through a windfall tax on banks. The umbrella body for unions, the TUC, has called for an increase in the bank surcharge to subsidise energy bills.All eyes will be on John Healey's first conference speech as chancellor on Monday.With borrowing costs for last month soaring to their second highest level, his room for manoeuvre is limited and he will not scoop his own Budget next month by announcing what is in it.But Labour activists will be keen to know from his language whether Healey's Treasury will opt for continuity or will represent a break from the past two years under Rachel Reeves, not just in rhetoric but reality.Some in Labour's ranks believe Burnham is planning for an early election, with party HQ recently launching "operation second term", to beef up its campaigning and organising strength.Burnham does not have to call an election until August 2029 - but going to the country early - perhaps as early as next spring - could deliver him a mandate of his own and free him from the constraints of Sir Keir Starmer's 2024 manifesto.Recent polling has suggested that a "Burnham bounce"  is real, though not dramatic. The party has moved from just under 20% in the polls at the end of the Starmer era to around the mid-twenties now.Ipsos puts its standing as high as 28%, external, while YouGov registers a more modest 23%, external. Labour strategists will be pleased that Reform UK's share – 21% in YouGov - is the lowest since January 2025,  and that Nigel Farage's party is now neck-and-neck with Kemi Badenoch's Conservatives. One Labour insider told me that Burnham is happy to see a resilient Badenoch, as this blunts Reform support and could point to a split vote on the right at an election.  And new research from YouGov, external suggests that at the all important constituency level, 63-68% of Lib Dem and Green voters would tactically vote for Labour to stop Reform UK winning their seat. Burnham of course also faces a challenge on the left. How much of a threat Zack Polanski's Greens can be in some traditional Labour seats will be tested in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election just a week after the Labour conference concludes.Downing Street insists that an early election is not being planned. To say anything else, though, would be to repeat the uncertainty of Gordon Brown's early months in No 10 when election speculation wasn't doused - and had become so rife that he was reputationally damaged when he decided not to go to the polls.But some who have been in regular touch with No 10 tell me they have seen no serious signs that an early election is in the offing. Burnham appears determined to give his government enough time in office to present tangible achievements to a sceptical electorate.   And with Labour still well below the 34% vote share it captured in 2024, many Labour MPs will be pushing the PM not to cut and run.So don't expect the centre point of Burnham's conference speech to be a message to his MPs to go back to their constituencies and prepare for a loss of some of their seats. But equally don't expect election speculation to subside at this conference.The Labour Party has tried and trusted methods of managing dissent at party conferences, when it comes to votes on party policy.But the coming week could see a concerted effort by some on the left to push for a complete ban on arms sales to Israel and for Israel's actions in Gaza to be described by Labour as a genocide.Those close to Burnham believe he has gained considerable credit by sanctioning the illegal Israeli settlements on the West Bank and won't need to go further.There is also some frustration that his government has not yet revised proposals to make migrants wait much longer to gain permanent residency rights, and there are genuine differences over whether the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields should go ahead.But while Burnham is facing some difficult calls, this is not a leader facing a restless party in revolt.He has offered to give the hard-pressed public "breathing space" amid a cost of living crisis.And his own party is so far giving him breathing space as leader – largely sighing with relief that it is not Sir Keir Starmer who will be delivering the main address this year.Senior Labour officials have hailed the forthcoming conference as an opportunity to "show voters a party that is boldly, confidently, and authentically Labour".But not too far below the political radar, there are already demands from some in the wider Labour movement to prove it.

schema.headline: New policies, election speculation: What to expect from Burnham's first Labour conference as PM

title: Greek PM Mitsotakis urges Burnham to return Elgin Marbles
description: The Greek prime minister has called on Andy Burnham to find the "political will" to send the Parthenon sculptures back to Greece. Kyriakos Mitsotakis
body: The Greek prime minister has called on Andy Burnham to find the "political will" to send the Parthenon sculptures back to Greece. Kyriakos Mitsotakis wrote in the Guardian that returning the classical treasures, also known as the Elgin Marbles in the UK, would "send a powerful signal" but would require "courage".The sculptures have been on display in the British Museum since the 19th Century, though Greece has long disputed the legality of their removal.Mitsotakis and his government have previously held talks with the British Museum about the sculptures, but the two have so far failed to reach an agreement, with Greek authorities seeking their permanent return.The Greek PM used the recent fanfare generated by the loan of the Bayeux Tapestry to the British Museum to restate his country's claim to the Elgin Marbles."Nobody would seriously contemplate cutting what survives of the tapestry in two and displaying half in London and half in Bayeux, and claiming this was an adequate way to understand it," he wrote on Thursday, external. "Yet that is exactly what happened to the Parthenon sculptures."His comments come after British Museum director Nicholas Cullinan suggested that the recent arrangement struck between the UK and France, after decades of rejected requests to borrow the medieval embroidery, offered hope of a deal with Greece over the Elgin Marbles.Mitsotakis said he was "surprised at the recent suggestion from the museum that the Bayeux Tapestry loan might provide a template for an agreement over the Parthenon sculptures", adding: "I do not believe it does.""Greece cannot accept any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum's ownership of the sculptures, or a scheme that would mean we 'borrow' parts of our own monument," he wrote.Instead, he urged Burnham to stand by his previous comments on the sculptures and find a way of returning them for good.This would be a "decisive step", Mitsotakis said, that would "reunite the sculptures and transform a historic dispute into a unique act of cultural friendship".Back in 2023, several years before he returned to government and became prime minister, Burnham said the sculptures should be returned to Greece with "no strings attached". For years, he supported a change in the law to allow for this. But last month, he told the Financial Times that "ultimately it's an issue for the British Museum", adding that "legally that's where that issue rests".British ambassador Lord Elgin was granted permission by the Ottoman Empire, the governing authority in Athens at the time, to remove some of the marble statues in the early 19th Century.They were created between 447BC and 432BC to decorate the Temple of Athena - what is now known as the Parthenon, in the Acropolis in Athens.After an 1816 parliamentary select committee deemed Elgin's actions legal, the sculptures entered the British Museum collection by an act of Parliament.The Greeks dispute their removal was lawful and the demands to return the statues have been vocal.The Parthenon gallery in the Acropolis Museum in the Greek capital was deliberately designed with spaces left for the sculptures in the British Museum.Back in 2023, George Osborne, then the museum chair, told the BBC he was looking for a "more co-operative arrangement" after "quite a bitter disagreement" with the Greeks for more than 200 years.Mitsotakis's latest comments appear to suggest a ramping up of rhetoric around the thorny issue once again.Last month, Greece's health minister told Breitbart News he would like to see US President Donald Trump pressure the British to return the Parthenon pieces.The British Museum's position - and that of the UK government - is that the law prevents the permanent return of items held in its collection, though loan agreements are common.Campaigners point out that the British Museum Act could be amended. However, the UK government has not signalled that this is a priority.

schema.headline: Greek PM Mitsotakis urges Burnham to return Elgin Marbles

title: Portugal 1-0 Wales: Craig Bellamy wants more from his side after narrow Portugal loss
description: Wales earned plaudits but Craig Bellamy wants more from his side, after admitting they were forced to suffer in their narrow 1-0 defeat in Portugal.Jo
body: Wales earned plaudits but Craig Bellamy wants more from his side, after admitting they were forced to suffer in their narrow 1-0 defeat in Portugal.Joao Felix's deflected strike proved enough to earn victory in Lisbon for the hosts, who also saw Cristiano Ronaldo's effort ruled out by VAR.It was a winning start to the Nations League title defence for Portugal and for new manager Jorge Jesus.Despite being under pressure for long spells in Lisbon, Bellamy's injury-hit side ended strongly as Brennan Johnson and Lewis Koumas both went close to snatching a draw."It was a difficult game for us. We had to suffer a lot," said Bellamy."I think that's the longest we've been in a game without the ball."We could have done more with the ball but I'm beyond proud as well. "We have a lot of players who weren't here. That's OK, we can handle it. "A lot of players who don't play, week-in, week-out. So for them to use the energy they were able to, we've got to have a big heart to be able to do that. They've always shown that and they showed that again."Ronaldo unsurprisingly took the spotlight in the build-up to the contest at Jose Alvalade Stadium - where the 41-year-old began his professional career with Sporting in 2002.The forward missed a big opportunity and had a goal disallowed for offside, which would have been his 980th top-flight goal, before being substituted midway through the second half.He could well line-up against Wales again when Portugal play the return match in Cardiff in November.Amid the noise around the Al-Nassr frontman, Bellamy refused to be overawed and hopes to face Ronaldo again."If you looked at everything that was going on, it's a £1.4bn squad you're up against, [but] I felt quite calm. The players give me that," added the Wales boss."Ronaldo is one of the greatest players of all generations, not just this generation. "You have to plan for him because he's beyond dangerous, even at his age. "He's a superstar and I'd love to think I'd have the opportunity to be up against him again, but I don't know, maybe time is ticking."

title: Hundreds of thousands expected in Paris for Pope Leo's visit
description: Pope Leo XIV embarks on a four-day visit to France on Friday, with the highpoint being a giant Mass attended by more than half a million people in cen
body: Pope Leo XIV embarks on a four-day visit to France on Friday, with the highpoint being a giant Mass attended by more than half a million people in central Paris.For Saturday's afternoon celebration, an altar has been built on the Place de la Concorde and a large area around the Champs-Élysées sealed off by police.Some 600,000 Catholic faithful are expected to cram the avenue up to the Arc de Triomphe and beyond.Large crowds are also due at other stages in the Pope's itinerary, reflecting an enthusiasm that the Church attributes to growing spiritual thirst among the French and other Europeans.President Emmanuel Macron greeted the Pope at Orly airport on Friday morning, and is due to hold talks with him at the Élysée Palace on geopolitical issues and artificial intelligence (AI) later. He will also deliver a speech with the Pope in Metz. However, the president will not be at any of the Pope's Masses, largely to avoid breaching France's strict separation of state and religion.Instead, the Champs-Élysées Mass will be attended by his wife Brigitte and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu. Several candidates for next year's presidential election are also due, including Marine Le Pen of the nationalist right, centrists Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, and conservative Bruno Retailleau.There were reports of tensions between Macron and the Vatican team sent to make arrangements, with the president allegedly frustrated in his wish for a more ceremonial aspect to the visit.On Monday the Pope will be in Metz, in northeast France, where he will pay tribute to Robert Schuman (1886-1963), a founding father of the European Union and a fervent Catholic who is today a candidate for beatification.The Pope will also meet a group of migrants in Paris, and in Lourdes some victims of sexual abuse by members of the Catholic clergy.Born in Chicago in 1955, Pope Leo XIV was originally called Robert Prevost – a French name.  In fact his paternal grandmother was born in Le Havre in Normandy in 1894. When she married in the US many years later she and her Italian husband took the name Prevost, which had been her mother's maiden-name.France has a historically complex relationship with the Catholic Church of Rome.  The country was long known as the "Eldest Daughter of the Church" because supposedly, but inaccurately, it was the first kingdom to convert to Christianity. Actually Armenia, Georgia and Ethiopia preceded it.In the 14th Century the papacy came in exile to Avignon in southern France, and over following centuries French armies periodically intervened in Italian politics, where popes were secular rulers as well as heads of the Church.  Napoleon held two popes in captivity.Recent popes have all come to France, most notably John-Paul II, who came several times between 1980 and 2004, and Pope Francis who came three times, but avoided Paris, going instead to Strasbourg, Marseilles and Corsica.Today France has secularised with the rest of Europe, and less than half of the population identifies as Catholic.The number of regular worshippers has fallen from 35% of the population in 1960 to less than 5% today, while the number of priests has shrunk by two-thirds from 25,000 in 1990 to fewer than 9,000.But in recent years there have been signs of a growing interest in religious tradition, with the number of adult baptisms more than doubling in five years to hit 10,000 in 2025."France has indeed secularised, but there is a void where God and values used to be," said Cardinal François Bustillo, Bishop of Ajaccio."People are searching for something. Maybe they go to India or Tibet or the Amazon. And now the Pope comes here from Rome, bringing a reminder to people of their own roots."It was John-Paul II who awoke the East. Now Leo XIV will awake the West," he said.

schema.headline: Hundreds of thousands expected in Paris for Pope Leo's visit

title: Netanyahu defends Israeli military action as delegates walk out before UN speech
description: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has fiercely defended his country's military campaigns in Iran, Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East in a s
body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has fiercely defended his country's military campaigns in Iran, Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East in a speech to the UN General Assembly. After dozens of delegates walked out in protest as he took to the stage, Netanyahu vowed to continue fighting: "We're going to win. We have no other choice."In response to the walkout, he said: "If there are any other moral cowards who haven't left the hall, please do so now."The Israeli leader also rejected accusations that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza.Hours earlier, in a recorded message Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas told the UN that Israeli policies - in particular the illegal expansion of Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank - threatened "the very life and existence of the Palestinian people on their homeland".He also said it jeopardised the two-state solution, which is an internationally backed formula for peace between Israel and the Palestinians.Abbas said that Palestinians were being subjected to "killing, destruction, starvation and attempts at displacement, as well as a genocidal war" in Gaza by the Israeli military.The Palestinian leader was addressing the annual gathering via a video link because he had been denied a US entry visa.Netanyahu, who is subject to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant for alleged war crimes, launched scathing attacks on nations and leaders who have criticised him."They accuse Israel, tiny Israel, of colonialism - some colonialism. And who's accusing us? Among them are people in Britain and in France. For God's sake, they invented the term," he said.He went on to label Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan a "tyrant", accusing him of supporting the Palestinian armed group Hamas.Erdogan told the UN on Tuesday that the injustices faced by those in Gaza and the West Bank "deeply offends the conscience of humanity".Netanyahu's comments drew a sharp response from the Turkish presidency's communications director Burhanettin Duran.The Israeli PM's use of the UN General Assembly podium to level "baseless accusations" against Turkey and Erdogan was incompatible with the UN's "ideals of peace, law and dialogue", Duran said, according to state-run news agency Anadolu. New York City's left-wing mayor Zohran Mamdani - who had previously vowed to arrest Netanyahu but later said he did not have the authority to do so - was also criticised by the Israeli leader."Since you were elected mayor of this city, many Jews no longer feel safe in New York," the Israeli prime minister said.In a statement, Mamdani's office said Netanyahu "used his speech to repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians".Netanyahu also thanked US President Donald Trump for his "bold leadership", referring to the air strikes the US and Israel jointly launched against Tehran in February."Israel and America acted together not only to protect ourselves, but to save civilisation," he said.Much of Netanyahu's speech was pitched at the two audiences he needs to convince the most: Israelis as he faces a critical election at home next month, and Americans as Israel faces growing isolation and fractures in support abroad. In Israel, Netanyahu's once unrivalled image as "Mr Security" has come under increasing scrutiny in what is the first election since the 7 October 2023 attacks. Some political opponents have argued he is unfit for office following Israeli media reports, firmly denied by Netanyahu, that he did not heed warnings of a potential attack by Hamas. His characteristic defiance at the UN podium will be replayed in a campaign seeing his religious-right wing coalition trailing in the polls. Netanyahu appeared to have pre-scripted his comments about "moral cowards" as he faced a mass walkout. It will likely be used as he tries once again to burnish an image as being the only Israeli politician that can truly take on Israel's growing number of global critics. There were also clearly marked references meant for American audiences, including the joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran and his praise for Trump. Netanyahu, who was born in Israel but spent his formative years in Pennsylvania, has always tried to present himself as having a unique ability to pitch Israel's case in the US. Despite continued weapons supply from Washington, he faces an increasingly sceptical public. Polls suggest plummeting support for Israel among Democrats, and a fracture in historically high levels of backing among Republicans which has spread to Trump's Maga base.

schema.headline: Netanyahu defends Israeli military action as delegates walk out before UN speech

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Xi urges rivals to coexist in peace' and 'It's on at last'
description: According to the Times, ministers are looking at ways to help poorer households with their energy bills, external to tackle fears of what the paper ca
body: According to the Times, ministers are looking at ways to help poorer households with their energy bills, external to tackle fears of what the paper calls a "winter cost of living crisis". Ahead of the budget, Chancellor John Healey is said to have asked officials for options to "cushion" households from price rises. Government sources are quoted as saying the chancellor wants to take a "hands on" approach, but warn that the "challenging" economic situation means any support is likely to be targeted.The Daily Telegraph leads on allegations regarding the care of the explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes., externalThe Guardian reports that there is at least a two-year delay for people in large parts of England waiting for autism assessments, external, due to surging demand. The paper says NHS care boards are struggling with the cost, and adopting different approaches to rationing assessments. The NHS Alliance's mental health director tells the Guardian that health leaders are "keenly aware" of the issues and working to address them.Downing Street advisors are said to be pushing for an election as soon as next year, external, reports the Daily Telegraph. However, one senior source is quoted as saying there is a "diverse" opinion across government about the timing of the next election. They add that Labour would be "naive not to be contemplating all scenarios".Sarah Ferguson, the former wife of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, has received "seven-figure offers" for her autobiography, external, according to the Sun. Publishing sources tell the paper she is "days away" from a deal.And the musician Rick Wakeman is pictured in the Guardian playing the piano to an audience of 150 bears in Vietnam., external The paper explains his performance at a sanctuary is aimed at raising awareness about bears being kept in terrible conditions. The former Yes keyboardist is said to have joked behind the mic: "Before you ask, I won't be playing teddy bear's picnic."

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Xi urges rivals to coexist in peace' and 'It's on at last'

title: Angh by Theja Rio at Toronto: The Indian film taking Nagaland to global cinema
description: There is something pleasingly improbable about Angh.The film comes from Nagaland, a mountainous state of fewer than two million people on India's nort
body: There is something pleasingly improbable about Angh.The film comes from Nagaland, a mountainous state of fewer than two million people on India's northeastern frontier, and is in Konyak, a tribal language unfamiliar to most Indians, never mind audiences abroad. It was director Theja Rio's first feature and most of its cast faced a camera for the first time.And yet, at the Toronto International Film Festival this month, this quiet film won the Platform Prize, a major juried award.The award is intended to recognise films with a particularly distinctive directorial voice. The jury praised Rio's "refreshing perspective" and the film's portrait of a world rarely encountered on the international screen.The win also gives Angh an unusual route towards the 2027 Academy Awards. Under new rules, winners of designated prizes at six international festivals can qualify for consideration in the International Feature Film category without relying solely on their country's official submission.This does not make Angh an Oscar nominee. But it does place a Konyak-language film from one of India's smallest states inside a global conversation from which such stories have been almost entirely absent.Rio still sounds slightly startled by it. When we speak in Delhi, roughly 72 hours after the win, he has barely had a moment to breathe - Toronto, flights, interviews, more interviews."There were a lot of good films in the competition", he says, including films by far more seasoned directors. His producers were confident. "They thought we were going to win. I wasn't."He is also less solemn than Angh might suggest. Before cinema, he wanted to be a rapper - "a kid from Compton instead of a kid from Nagaland", as he puts it. His tastes still range happily from Black Thought, the lead rapper of American hip-hop group The Roots, to his favourite filmmaker, the Iranian director Abbas Kiarostami.But for his first feature, he turned close to home.Set in the early 1960s, Angh follows Anghba, the ageing hereditary chief of a Konyak village, and his young son, as the world around them changes. The Konyaks are one of Nagaland's 17 major tribes, concentrated in the eastern district of Mon, where such chiefs are known as Anghs. Even today, some older men bear facial tattoos associated with the Konyaks' historical practice of headhunting.Anghba and his son are among the last in their region to hold to an ancestral faith as Christianity spreads.Then an American missionary, played by Scottish actor Douglas Henshall, arrives. The father resists but the son is now curious.Rio says the idea for the film came a few years ago, when he was visiting Mon for another project. What struck him was how closely different generations seemed to live alongside one another there. Within a single family, he says, a grandfather might be a former headhunter, his face still tattooed; two generations later, his grandson might play guitar in a rock band."It feels like you've jumped on a time machine," Rio says. "The past and the present sort of coexist together."The year also matters. Nagaland, which was earlier part of Assam state, formally became an Indian state in December 1963, during a period of profound political and social change. By then, Christianity had been spreading among Naga communities for decades, bringing changes extending beyond religious belief into customs, rituals and everyday life.Dr B Amo Konyak, a scholar of Konyak society, says the changes during this period were almost like a disappearance.Some practices were lost; others "survived in fragments" - in the memories of elders, in family heirlooms. What had once been part of everyday life became heritage.But Dr Konyak says culture did not simply stop. People carried parts of it into new religious and social worlds. Traditions survived, but changed meaning as they changed form.It's this moment of transition that Rio wanted to capture. "The past 50 or 60 years have brought extraordinary churn," he says, widening the distance between generations.In Angh, he explores this through the relationship between the father and son who "intimately love and care about each other very deeply", even as their worlds begin to pull apart.Critic Siddhant Adlakha was struck by the ambiguity the film captures. "Progress and tradition can be nonlinear, even entwined," he says, "rather than strictly opposing forces."The film is yet to reach a wider audience, but its brief trailer offers a glimpse of how Rio constructed this world. Mist hangs over steep green hills; figures move through forests and village paths; fire and lamplight pick faces out of the darkness. The landscape is beautiful but not merely picturesque - a small world held together by ritual, family and geography, while something larger presses in from beyond its edges.Adlakha singles out the quiet close-ups of Anghlong Konyak, the first-time actor who plays the chief, and the "gentleness" with which Rio captures his "subdued rage".What the camera saw mattered almost as much as where it was looking from.Konyak people have long been viewed from the outside. Dr Konyak points to explorers, colonial officials, missionaries and photographers drawn to tattooed faces, ornaments, weapons and headhunting, while the lives behind them often receded from view.Rio was conscious of inheriting that history. "There have been several films and documentaries made about Nagaland," he says, "but these sort of films tend to follow the gaze of the explorer rather than the subject."With Angh, he wanted to reverse that gaze, asking viewers to "step inside the shoes of these characters".The change is subtle but consequential. The Konyaks are no longer an exotic remnant of the past, but people living through what Dr Konyak describes as "love, grief, conflict, faith, uncertainty and generational change".Konyak advisers worked on dialogue, costume and production design, and much of the cast was drawn from first-time Konyak performers. The forest, too, belongs to the people moving through it. Adlakha says Rio treats it "not just as a setting, but as a home with a history", much as an urban filmmaker might treat Mumbai or New York.Rio and cinematographer Adam Pietkiewicz shot Angh on 16mm film, drawing on photographs and footage of missionaries and Naga communities from the 1950s and 60s. They wanted to recreate the grain, texture and atmosphere of those archival images, while shifting the point of view from outsider to subject.It was an evocative choice - and a logistical headache. Unlike digital footage, the exposed film could not simply be reviewed on set. Every four or five days, the cans had to be sent to Mumbai for processing, while the crew carried on shooting without knowing exactly what they had captured.There were more prosaic problems too.During a night shoot with Henshall, an old Second World War Jeep was supposed to be driven into frame. It behaved perfectly through rehearsals. But when the cameras began rolling, the engine refused to start. After repeated attempts, the crew managed to capture just one take of the Jeep entering the frame."It was a very difficult night," Rio says.Angh may be Rio's first feature, but its journey places it within a widening map of Indian cinema, especially in the northeast.Adlakha points to filmmakers such as Assam's Rima Das and Meghalaya's Dominic Sangma whose work, he says, reveals "how complex and multifaceted the idea of Indian cinema happens to be".Rio thinks Nagaland still remains at the edge of that scene. Its film industry is, as he puts it, "at a very nascent stage", with little of the reach enjoyed by India's established filmmaking centres.But he hopes some of the attention around Angh travels back with it.There are, he says, "so many talented filmmakers with so many beautiful stories that are yet to be told".For now, though, Rio is looking forward to something more ordinary - getting back to Nagaland."I want to play football with my friends."

schema.headline: Angh by Theja Rio at Toronto: The Indian film taking Nagaland to global cinema

title: Zinedine Zidane waited for France - now what will he bring to role?
description: Zidane waited for France - now can he harness their star power?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Zinedine Zidane won the Champions League three
body: Zidane waited for France - now can he harness their star power?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Zinedine Zidane won the Champions League three times as Real Madrid managerByRaphael JucobinFrench football writerUpdated 3 hours agoFrance will have a new face on the touchline for the first time in 14 years when they face Turkey on Friday.Zinedine Zidane replaced Didier Deschamps after France's fourth-place finish at the World Cup, but his appointment had been an open secret long before Les Bleus' third-place play-off loss to England.Talks between the former Real Madrid manager and the French football authorities kicked off as early as February 2025 - after Zidane's former team-mate Deschamps announced a few weeks earlier he would step down following the 2026 World Cup.When he was unveiled in Paris, Zidane was keen to highlight the time he had spent waiting on the sidelines and preparing for the job."I had several offers in the last four or five years, but I turned them all down," an emotional Zidane said. "The national team is the only thing I wanted."While his enthusiasm at taking the job was the overarching theme of his first news conference in the French capital, the midfield legend offered few clues to France fans as to how he would approach the role.Even a question on Kylian Mbappe's captaincy was bypassed: "The most important thing for him now is to rest, we'll have the chance to speak in September."Mbappe, speaking to Spanish newspaper AS, has since said having the former Real Madrid star as his national team coach was "like a film".When asked about his preferred style of play, Zidane opted against going into tactical detail."I can't explain to you in just a couple of words how we're going win. I have to arrive, meet with the players, and explain my plans to them. After that, it'll be up to me to keep this team winning."However, Zidane confirmed his intention "to do things differently" and he has called up five uncapped players for this international break.He went on to signal that there would be a degree of "continuation" from the work of his predecessor, which he made sure to praise."I'm going to try do what I know how to, but it won't be a complete break either."So what will Zidane bring to the France dugout?Zidane the playerZidane, who retired in 2006, was one of the most exciting attacking midfielders of his generation. He won league titles and European trophies with Juventus and Real Madrid, while he helped France to victory at the 1998 World Cup and Euro 2000.Zidane started his career at Cannes and then moved to Bordeuax. He almost joined Premier League side Blackburn Rovers in 1995, but the move broke down with Rovers owner Jack Walker reportedly asking manager Kenny Dalglish: "Why do you want to sign Zidane when we have Tim Sherwood?"Instead Zidane moved to Juventus, winning six trophies, before he was signed by Real Madrid for a then record £45.8m.For France he was the hero of the home 1998 World Cup, scoring twice in the final, a 3-0 win over Brazil and was named the best player at Euro 2000.He retired after the 2006 World Cup, a campaign full of highs, leading France to the final, and one big low, when his playing career ended after he was sent off in the showpiece match for headbutting Italy defender Marco Materazzi.Zidane the managerZidane and Deschamps - two 1998 World Cup winners - do share a few similar traits in their management, not least in their pragmatism, as well as the laissez-faire approach to attacking phases which Deschamps embraced in the recent World Cup.Given the attacking talent at his disposal, it stands to reason that Zidane would carry on in that vein."I was a number 10 as a player," he said, hinting he would retain the role Michael Olise thrived in for much of the summer."What motivates me is the game, it's scoring goals," he added.With the team netting 20 times in North America, Deschamps has arguably laid the foundations for his successor's attacking set-up.Zidane is finding Les Bleus in immeasurably better shape than his predecessor did at the start of his own tenure, at which point the wounds of the 2010 World Cup fiasco were still fresh.The appointment does come with a degree of uncertainty, though.Given that Zidane has spent five years out of management, and the Real Madrid job is the only other senior coaching role of his career, it might seem like a gamble.The 54-year-old himself has acknowledged leading a national team would be an entirely new proposition: "It's new to me, but I'm not scared. This is what I wanted."Predictably, the reaction among players and fans to Zidane's arrival has been almost unanimously positive. He was met with a crowd of supporters carrying flares and banners as he left the French Football Federation's headquarters after his unveiling."Welcome home," Mbappe wrote on Instagram later in the day.'A great day for French football'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Zidane was met by fans and media after his unveiling as France boss"It's a great day for French football," his former France and Bordeaux team-mate Bixente Lizarazu told France Info later that day. "He is more than fit to manage Les Bleus, given what he did at Real Madrid with great players and big egos."The respect that the former Ballon d'Or winner commands in a dressing room is one of his key strengths.Even more so than Deschamps, a France legend in his own right, Zidane is a figure who can rival - perhaps even overshadow - his own players in terms of star power.In this sense, he may be the ideal manager to get the most out of an attack made up of Mbappe, Ousmane Dembele, Desire Doue and Olise.This international break - lasting four Nations League fixtures over three weeks - will offer the France players a crash-course to the new management style.After facing Turkey, they have two games against Belgium and one against Italy in Paris.Given his iconic status within French football and on the wider national stage, Zidane will invariably enjoy an unprecedented degree of goodwill regardless of his initial results.Whether he uses that leeway to experiment tactically and bring in new faces remains to be seen.His homecoming at the Stade de France on Friday, 2 October, against the Azzurri no less, is an ideal fixture to begin the new era.A version of this article was first published on 28 July.

schema.headline: Zinedine Zidane waited for France - now what will he bring to role?

title: UK summer 2026: BBC postcode lookup shows how hot and dry it was
description:
Where does the data come from?
                                            This lookup uses data from the Had
body:
Where does the data come from?
                                            This lookup uses data from the HadUK Grid dataset 
                            
                            
                         (opens in new tab), which is produced by the Met Office Hadley Centre. HadUK Grid is one of the main products used by scientists to monitor and research the UK’s changing climate.
                                            The HadUK dataset displays temperature and rainfall data across a uniform grid covering the entire landmass of the UK. The data does not cover the Channel Islands. Every value on the grid is an estimate for the centre point of a 1km by 1km grid box, the most detailed climate data publicly available for the UK. The values are created using observations from land-based weather stations across the country, and by taking into account additional factors such as altitude, terrain and distance from the coast to scientifically “fill in the gaps” between weather stations.
                                            The results displayed for each grid area represents a mean average of that grid cell and its nearest grid cells. For most areas, this represents a 5km square centred on the primary grid cell. Along irregular coastlines and on small islands, the nearest grid cells are chosen to match the shape of the coastline or island, but no cells are further than 7km away.
                                                This approach aims to avoid sharp jumps between neighbouring locations which may occasionally arise due to uncertainties in the data, while still making use of the most detailed dataset available to capture local weather conditions across the UK's varied geography.
                                            The data for 2026 is provisional, with fewer observations feeding into calculations due to lags in data availability. As such, the precise values could change slightly in future as more data comes available. The historical averages are calculated over a 30-year period from 1991-2020, which matches the standard period used by the UN’s World Meteorological Organization.
                                        What does the weather data represent?
                                            The average temperature represents the mean average of the selection of grid cells across the month or season.
                                            The maximum temperature is the mean average of the daily maximums recorded across all nearest grid cells for the month or season; the minimum temperature is the mean average of the daily minimums.
                                            The rainfall is the total amount of rain for the month or season, averaged across the selection of grid cells.
                                        Acknowledgements
                                            Methodology support from Dan Hollis, Amy Doherty and Oli Claydon, UK Met Office.

schema.headline: UK summer 2026: BBC postcode lookup shows how hot and dry it was
